title: Mock 1 · Foundations
blurb: All 22 chapters at entry level, with the core SIF facts every V-D candidate must know.

questions.q: Which of the following risks can be substantially reduced by holding a well-diversified portfolio of stocks?
options: Inflation risk on the whole portfolio
Risk arising from a change in monetary policy
questions.explanation: Total risk = systematic + unsystematic. Diversification eliminates a major part of unsystematic (specific) risk; systematic risk can only be hedged, e.g., with index futures.
hints: Correct — diversification removes stock/industry-specific risk.
Wrong — market risk remains even in a diversified portfolio.
Wrong — inflation hits all assets; diversification across stocks does not remove it.
Wrong — policy changes are a systematic, market-wide factor.

questions.q: An investor wants to invest in Specialized Investment Fund (SIF) strategies of a single AMC. What is the minimum investment requirement?
options: ₹10 lakh in each investment strategy separately
₹10 lakh across all investment strategies of that AMC
questions.explanation: SIF minimum investment is ₹10 lakh from the investor across all investment strategies of the same AMC.
hints: Wrong — the threshold is aggregate across strategies, not per strategy.
Wrong — ₹50 lakh is the PMS-type figure, not SIF.
Wrong — no ₹1 crore threshold is prescribed for SIF in the workbook.
Correct — the workbook sets the ₹10 lakh threshold at investor level across all strategies of the same AMC.

questions.q: Under the Equity Long-Short Fund strategy of an SIF, the minimum investment in equity and equity-related instruments is:
questions.explanation: Equity Long-Short Fund: minimum 80% in equity & equity-related instruments; maximum 25% unhedged short exposure through derivatives.
hints: Wrong — 65% is the floor for the Equity Ex-Top 100 Long-Short strategy (outside top 100 stocks).
Wrong — 25% is the cap on unhedged short exposure.
Correct — Equity Long-Short requires at least 80% in equity and equity-related instruments.
Wrong — 95% is the floor for index funds/ETFs and FoFs.

questions.q: As per SEBI MF Regulations 2026, the minimum net worth an asset management company must maintain is:
questions.explanation: The AMC needs a net worth of not less than ₹50 crore (effective 1 Jan 2024); the sponsor must ensure it is maintained continuously.
hints: Wrong — ₹10 crore is the sponsor's average-profit test, not AMC net worth.
Correct — AMC net worth must be at least ₹50 crore, maintained continuously.
Wrong — ₹25 crore is not the current requirement.
Wrong — ₹100 crore is not the prescribed figure.

questions.q: Which regulation of the SEBI MF Regulations 2026 specifies the permissible investments of a Specialized Investment Fund?
questions.explanation: Per Regulation 51, an SIF may invest in instruments permitted under Regulation 39 for MF schemes, subject to the Sixth Schedule restrictions.
hints: Wrong — Regulation 11 deals with trustee eligibility.
Correct — Regulation 51 lays down SIF investment limits (Reg 39 universe, subject to the Sixth Schedule).
Wrong — 22(9)(c) deals with changes in fundamental attributes.
Wrong — 66(6) relates to AMC paying distribution commission.

questions.q: How many levels of risk does the SIF 'Risk-Band' have?
questions.explanation: Since SIFs are riskier than other MF schemes, their risk is shown on a separate Risk-Band with five levels.
hints: Wrong — six levels belong to the mutual fund risk-o-meter.
Wrong — there are five levels, not four.
Correct — Risk-Band runs from level 1 (lowest) to level 5 (highest).
Wrong — there are five levels, not three.

questions.q: According to the SEBI Master Circular of 20 March 2026, how are mutual fund distributors to be remunerated by AMCs?
options: Only through trail commission, with no upfront commission
Upfront commission at the time of each purchase
A share of the AMC's profits
questions.explanation: AMCs shall adopt a full trail model of commission in all schemes, without any upfront commission or upfronting of trail (cash or kind).
hints: Correct — AMCs must follow the full trail model; no upfronting of trail directly or indirectly.
Wrong — upfront commission is prohibited.
Wrong — no retainer model is prescribed.
Wrong — profit-sharing is not a permitted distribution payout.

questions.q: An NFO of an open-ended scheme other than ELSS can remain open for subscription for a maximum of:
questions.explanation: NFOs stay open for at least 3 working days and, other than ELSS, at most 15 days; allotment/refund within 5 business days of closure.
hints: Wrong — 3 working days is the minimum period.
Wrong — 30 days exceeds the cap.
Wrong — 45 days exceeds the cap.
Correct — the maximum NFO period (other than ELSS) is 15 days.

questions.q: Which statement about subscription and redemption frequency is correct?
options: They must be the same for MF schemes, but may differ for SIF investment strategies
They must be the same for all MF schemes and SIF strategies
They may differ for all MF schemes
They must be daily for every SIF strategy
questions.explanation: Subscription and redemption frequency must be the same for all MF schemes except SIFs, where they can be distinct (e.g., daily purchase, weekly redemption).
hints: Correct — the workbook allows SIF strategies, e.g., daily subscriptions with weekly redemptions.
Wrong — SIF is the stated exception.
Wrong — regular MF schemes must keep them the same.
Wrong — debt/hybrid SIFs redeem weekly or twice a week, not daily.

questions.q: An investment of ₹1,000 grows to ₹4,000 in 2 years. What is the compounded annual return?
hints: Wrong — 150% is the simple return (300%) divided by 2.
Wrong — 300% is the absolute (simple) return over 2 years.
Wrong — 75% does not follow from the CAGR formula.

questions.q: Why does the direct plan of a scheme usually show a higher NAV than its regular plan over time?
options: It invests in a different portfolio
It carries a higher exit load
It is exempt from capital gains tax
Its expense ratio is lower because no distributor commission is built in
questions.explanation: Direct and regular plans have the same portfolio; the direct plan's lower TER (no commission) leads to a higher NAV.
hints: Wrong — both plans share the same portfolio.
Wrong — exit load does not raise NAV.
Wrong — tax treatment is identical for both plans.
Correct — direct plans exclude distribution commission, so TER is lower and NAV compounds faster.

questions.q: An index option is best described as a:
questions.explanation: A derivative derives its value from an underlying — here, a stock index.
hints: Wrong — it carries no debt obligation.
Correct — its value is derived from the underlying index.
Wrong — cash market products involve the underlying itself.
Wrong — money market instruments are short-term debt.

questions.q: A jewellery exporter who sells gold futures to protect the value of the gold inventory she already holds is acting as a:
questions.explanation: Hedgers face price risk on underlying assets and use derivatives to reduce it.
hints: Correct — she has an existing exposure and uses derivatives to reduce risk.
Wrong — a speculator takes on risk to profit from a price view.
Wrong — an arbitrageur exploits price differences across markets.
Wrong — a market maker quotes two-way prices; that is not her role.

questions.q: Sensex and Nifty are currently computed on which methodology?
options: Full market capitalisation without float adjustment
questions.explanation: Most global indices, including Sensex, Nifty and SX40, have moved to the free-float market capitalisation method.
hints: Wrong — Dow Jones and Nikkei 225 are price-weighted.
Wrong — equal weighting is a different design.
Correct — Indian indices (Sensex, Nifty, SX40) moved to free-float basis.
Wrong — they were earlier full market-cap weighted, but now use free float.

questions.q: You sold one stock futures contract at ₹1,450 (lot size 500) and later bought it back at ₹1,412. What is your profit or loss?
questions.explanation: Short futures P&L = (Sell price − Buy price) × lot = 38 × 500 = ₹19,000.
hints: Wrong — a short gains when price falls.
Wrong — ₹38,000 doubles the lot.
Wrong — multiplying by 0.38% of price is wrong.
Correct — (1,450 − 1,412) × 500 = ₹19,000 gain for a short position.

questions.q: Margins in equity futures trading are paid by:
options: Both the buyer and the seller
questions.explanation: Both buyers and sellers of futures pay initial margin because both have an obligation to honour the contract.
hints: Wrong — the seller is also obligated.
Correct — both sides have an obligation, so both deposit initial margin.
Wrong — the buyer is also obligated.
Wrong — the clearing corporation collects margins; it does not pay them.

questions.q: A call option is in-the-money when:
options: The spot price is below the strike price
The spot price equals the strike price
The spot price is above the strike price
The premium exceeds the strike price
questions.explanation: Call ITM: strike < spot; put ITM: strike > spot.
hints: Wrong — that makes a call out-of-the-money.
Wrong — that is at-the-money.
Correct — exercising immediately would give a positive cash flow.
Wrong — moneyness compares spot and strike, not premium.

questions.q: You buy a put option with a strike of ₹520 at a premium of ₹18. What is the break-even price at expiry?
questions.explanation: Break-even for a put = Strike − Premium = 520 − 18 = ₹502.
hints: Wrong — 538 is strike + premium (call BEP).
Wrong — at 520 you would lose the full premium.
Wrong — the premium is the maximum loss, not the BEP.
Correct — put BEP = strike − premium = 520 − 18.

questions.q: An investor buys a call with a lower strike and sells a call with a higher strike on the same stock and expiry. This strategy is a:
questions.explanation: Bullish vertical spread using calls: buy the lower-strike call and sell the higher-strike call (net debit).
hints: Wrong — a bear call spread shorts the lower strike.
Correct — long lower-strike call + short higher-strike call = bullish vertical spread.
Wrong — a straddle combines a call and a put at the same strike.
Wrong — a calendar spread uses different expiries.

questions.q: Which strategy combines a long stock position with a long put on the same stock?
questions.explanation: A protective put limits downside to the premium (plus any strike gap) while keeping upside; its payoff resembles a long call.
hints: Correct — long stock + long put insures the holding against a fall.
Wrong — a covered call sells a call against the stock.
Wrong — a short strangle sells OTM calls and puts.
Wrong — a bear put spread uses two puts and no stock.

questions.q: If market interest rates rise, the price of an existing fixed-coupon bond will generally:
options: Rise only if it is a zero-coupon bond
questions.explanation: The price-yield relationship is inverse; higher yields mean lower present value of fixed cash flows.
hints: Wrong — prices rise when yields fall.
Wrong — prices change with yields.
Correct — bond prices and yields move inversely.
Wrong — zero-coupon bonds fall even more because of their longer duration.

questions.q: An interest rate cap is best described as:
options: A series of interest rate put options
A series of interest rate call options
questions.explanation: Cap = series of interest rate calls (caplets); floor = series of puts; collar = buy cap + sell floor.
hints: Wrong — a series of puts is a floor.
Wrong — an FRA fixes one future period's rate.
Wrong — a swap exchanges cash flows; it is not an option.
Correct — a cap is a strip of caplets that pay when the rate exceeds the strike.

questions.q: One lot of a cash-settled GOI bond futures contract represents bonds with a face value of:
questions.explanation: Bond IRF unit of trading: 1 lot = FV ₹2 lakh = 2,000 bonds; contract value = price × 2,000.
hints: Correct — 1 lot = notional bonds of FV ₹2 lakh, i.e., 2,000 bonds of ₹100.
Wrong — the lot is ₹2 lakh, not ₹1 lakh.
Wrong — ₹5 crore is the wholesale cash-market lot (250 futures lots).
Wrong — ₹10 lakh is not the IRF lot.

questions.q: How is the 91-day T-bill futures contract quoted?
options: As the annualised discount yield itself
As the clean price of the T-bill
questions.explanation: 91-day T-bill futures: quotation = 100 − futures discount yield; contract value = 2,000 × (100 − 0.25y).
hints: Wrong — the quote converts the yield into a price-like number.
Correct — e.g., a 5% discount yield is quoted as 95.0000.
Wrong — T-bills are zero-coupon; the quote is 100 − yield.
Wrong — adding the yield is the wrong direction.

questions.q: An option that can be exercised only on certain specified dates before expiry is called a(n):
questions.explanation: Option styles: European (expiry only), American (any time), Bermudan (specified dates).
hints: Wrong — European options are exercisable only on expiry.
Wrong — American options can be exercised on any day up to expiry.
Wrong — Asian options are not discussed as an exercise style here.
Correct — Bermudan options sit between European and American in flexibility.
